newsitem.title: USA: U.S. econonomic strength boosts dlr - OMB's Minarik.
newsitem.headline: U.S. econonomic strength boosts dlr - OMB's Minarik.

text.p: A U.S. budget official Thursday attributed the dollar's buoyancy in recent months in part to the relative strength of the U.S. economy and voiced hopes growth in Europe and Asia will pick up in the future.

"The dollar is set by market forces," Joseph Minarik, Associate Director at the Office of Management and Budget, told Reuters Financial Television. "And among those forces is the strength of the U.S. economy relative to other economies."
He noted that the U.S. economy has been comparatively strong in the past few months.
The dollar has also been "bid up somewhat" by the good performance of U.S. exports and the attractiveness of U.S. financial markets to foreign investors, Minarik said.

"But our economy is staying on even keel," he said, "and over a period of time the international markets for currencies are going to take care of that and will have the dollar at a sustainable level so long as the fundamentals of our economy remain strong. And we're very confident of that," he added.
The dollar fell sharply on Thursday on comments by a senior Japanese official, but it is still is nearly 40 percent higher than record lows set against the yen last year.
Minarik acknowledged that "softness" in U.S. exports helped slow overall U.S. economic growth in the third quarter to a 2.2 percent annual rate from 4.7 percent in the second.

"But we think that in the future, as we look to hopefully continued and strengthening recovery in the major economies of Europe and Asia, ... we'll continue to see the export growth that we need to meet our overall growth targets," he said.
The administration has forecast U.S. growth of 2.3 percent in 1997 and beyond. "We expect that on a sustained basis, out into the future, we can meet and perhaps beat (that)," he said.
The budget official also said he saw no apparent upward pressure on prices despite low unemployment.
Minarik said that the three percent rise in the consumer price index over the past year or so probably overstates the underlying trend because of a rise in crude oil prices.
"If the crude market moves back down to $18 a barrel, we'd then get some help on the cpi, possibly below trend," he added.
